documentation.range:
Olive Baboons are the most extensively distributed of the baboons. They range throughout the Sahelian woodland and forest-mosaic habitats from southern Mauritania and Mali eastward through the Sudan to central Somalia. The range extends southwards as far as the Democratic Republic of Congo and Tanzania. Outlying populations inhabit the Tibesti and Air massifs in the Sahara (in Niger and Chad) and in the Pare and Usambara Mountains of Tanzania.

In East Africa, the distribution appears to be actively changing. In fact, wherever the range of Olive Baboons encounters that of other Papio species, there are hybrid zones. For example, Olive Baboons form a narrow hybrid zone with P. hamadryas below the Awash Falls and elsewhere in northern Ethiopia and hybridize with P. cynocephalus in the eastern part of Tsavo and Amboseli National Parks in Kenya.

In the clinal hybrid zone of P. anubis x P. cynocephalus between Laikipia District, just to the northeast and east of Mt. Kenya, and the Lower Tana River, near the Kenya coast, the baboons are intermediate and cannot be readily allocated to either P. anubis or P. cynocephalus. They become increasingly “yellow-like” in their phenotypes towards the Kenya Coast (De Jong and Butynski 2009, Zinner 2013). Papio anubis x P. cynocephalus hybrids are found near the Pare and Usambara Mountains in Tanzania. They are sympatric with a number of other primate species, including Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), Chlorocebus spp., several Cercopithecus species and Erythrocebus patas, across their range.
documentation.population: The Olive Baboon is widespread and locally common despite trapping, shooting and poisoning campaigns in parts of their range.
documentation.habitats:
The Olive Baboon inhabits a wide variety of habitats, including semi-desert, thorn scrub and open savanna. Most often, however, they are found in woodland and forest-mosaic habitats that may include high-elevation forest, gallery forest and rainforest up to 2,500 m in elevation. They are also found in rocky hills; some populations live in broad areas where woodlands have overtaken volcanic rock craters, such as those seen in northeastern Nigeria (Wallis pers. obs. 2005). They can readily persist in secondary and/or highly fragmented vegetation, including cultivated areas. Because water is a limiting factor, troops will travel long distances to find it. On occasion, they dig into semi-dry riverbeds to make small pools to access water.

Olive Baboons are omnivorous opportunists; their diet varies and adapts according to region, season and time of day. They eat mainly fruits and leaves, as well as flowers, seeds, shoots, buds, tuberous roots, bark, bulbs, twigs, sap, mushrooms and lichens (Zinner 2013). In dry seasons, they may use fallback foods such as resin, gum and bark. Olive Baboons eat animal prey, including a variety of invertebrates, lizards, birds, reptile and bird eggs and small mammals. The later include some primate species such as infant Chlorocebus spp. When meat-eating occurs, it typically involves randomly “stumbling” upon the item and eating it. Rarely does active hunting occur. When it does, it is individual hunting and not a cooperative organized group hunting such as that seen in Chimpanzees (Palombit 2013).

Because they often live near human habitations, Olive Baboons raid crops and garbage dumps. Thus, their diet can also include a variety of cultivated crops such as sugarcane, corn, bananas and beans. Crop-raiding can vary considerably; peaks in consumption may be associated with forest fruit shortages in some areas (see Naughton-Treves et al. 1998).

The species typically forages in extended, well-spaced troops that may occasionally number up to 200 animals, although more typically average about 80 individuals. As with most other baboons, the species is not territorial but instead uses home ranges that may overlap with other troops’ ranges. Home ranges vary in size and daily movements are usually less than 7 km (Zinner 2013). In addition to food and water, home ranges must contain suitable sleeping sites. For Olive Baboons, these typically require large trees and rocky outcroppings.

Olive Baboons typically live in multimale-multifemale troops, although some uni-male troops have been reported in West Africa. Extensive review and summary of the Olive Baboon’s social structure, behaviour, anatomy and reproduction may be found in Palombit (2013) and Zinner (2013).
documentation.threats:
There are currently no major threats to this species that reduce population numbers across its range. However, some populations are under local pressure from agriculture and development projects. Although not well documented, they are hunted for bushmeat in some areas (Wallis pers. obs. Tanzania 1991, Wallis pers. obs. in Nigeria 2006–2008, van Vliet et al. 2012). The potential for increased hunting pressure should be monitored. With rising numbers in the human population and declining numbers of other wildlife species, Olive Baboons may eventually become a more sought-after target; at 30 kg, an adult male provides a substantial source of protein. It should be noted that Olive Baboons have been found to harbour Simian Immunodeficiency Viruses (SIV) (Peeters et al. 2002) and Ebola virus (Leroy et al. 2004), thus highlighting the health risks of baboon meat consumption to humans.

Both Papio anubis and P. cynocephalus are naturally infected with Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, the bacterium that causes human yaws and closely related to the bacterium that causes syphilis (T. p. pallidum) (see Harper et al. 2012, Chuma et al. 2019). In Papio sp., the infection appears to spread through sexual contact and is associated with open lesions in and around the genitalia of both sexes. The degree of morbidity varies, including some cases of deaths occurring in the Tanzania’s Gombe National Park’s Olive Baboons, when the genitalia are so badly damaged that urinary flow was obstructed (Wallis and Lee 1999). Similar lesions appear in some other Olive Baboon populations throughout their range, most notably in Lake Manyara National Park in Tanzania (Chuma et al. 2019) and Yankari Game Reserve in Nigeria (Wallis pers. obs. 2007).

Thus, although hunting pressure, persecution for crop-raiding and incidence of disease transmission do not currently constitute “major threats”, both phenomena merit attention and monitoring.
documentation.measures:
This species is listed under Appendix II of CITES and as Vermin under the African Convention.

Olive Baboons are found in a many protected areas across their range. These include: Pendjari National Park in Benin; west of the Niger National Park in Burkina Faso; Bénoué, Bouba Ndjida and Waza National Parks, Faro Reserve and Kimbe River and Mbi Crater Game Reserves in Cameroon; Zakouma National Park in Chad; Garamba, Kahuzi-Biega and Virunga National Parks and Tayna Gorilla Reserve in the Democratic Republic of Congo; Awash and Bale Mountains National Parks, Stephanie Wildlife Sanctuary and Menagesha-Suba National Forest in Ethiopia; Bui, Digya and Mole National Parks, Kogyae Strict Nature Reserve, Bomfobiri Wildlife Sanctuary and Willi Falls Reserve in Ghana; Marahoué, Comoé and Mount Peko National Parks in Cote d’Ivoire; Lake Nakuru, Marsabit, Meru, Nairobi and Samburu National Parks and Masai Mara Game Reserve in Kenya; West National Park in Niger; Cross River, Gashaka-Gumti and Kainji Lake National Parks, Ngel Nyaki Forest Reserve, Yankari Game Reserve in Nigeria; Akagera, Nyungwe and Volcanoes National Parks in Rwanda; Dinder National Park in Sudan; Nimule National Park in South Sudan; Arusha, Gombe, Kilimanjaro, Lake Manyara, Serengeti and Tarangire National Parks in Tanzania; Keran and Fazao-Malfacassa National Parks and Koue Reserve in Togo; and Bwindi Impenetrable, Kibale, Murchison Falls and Queen Elizabeth National Parks and Budongo Forest Reserve in Uganda (Zinner 2013).

As mentioned under Threats, the Olive Baboon may see local population pressure from trapping due to crop-raiding and bushmeat use. They are also susceptible to the spread of Treponema pallidum, which can have debilitating or even deadly consequences. Thus, research and ongoing monitoring for hunting pressure and disease transmission is recommended.

The isolated subpopulations on Saharan massifs in Niger and Chad, as well as the area of the Pare mountains in Tanzania merit further protection and research. Research into their range, boundaries and hybridization could be useful for conservation planning. Attention should be given to the likely effects of climate change on ecosystem distribution across much of the Olive Baboon’s range (see Ponce-Reyes et al. 2017 for suggested study approaches).
documentation.use_trade: Hunting of Olive Baboons occurs in parts of their range, particularly in the west. There is no indication that their trade – as bushmeat – occurs beyond local or regional use, however.
documentation.rationale: Papio anubis is listed as Least Concern as the species is very widespread and abundant. It is often persecuted as a crop raider and hunted for bushmeat in some locations. However, there are currently no major threats believed to be resulting in a range-wide population decline.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
This species was previously treated as a subspecies of Papio hamadryas, but now is considered a species (Kingdon 1997, Groves 2001, 2005, Grubb et al. 2003). There are some regional differences in morphology and pelage colour, but there are no currently recognised subspecies (Zinner 2013).

Papio anubis hybridizes with P. cynocephalus in a broad clinal zone between Laikipia district to the northeast of Mont Kenya and the Lower Tana River near the Kenya coast. In that 200-km wide area, baboons are intermediate in appearance and are difficult to allocate to either species (Zinner 2013). Hybridization with P. papio is likely but has not been confirmed. Hybridization with Theropithecus gelada has been observed in the wild and even hybridization with White-naped Mangabeys (Cercocebus lunulatus) is suspected (R. Matsuda Goodwin pers. comm. 2020).

According to a review presented by Zinner (2013), P. anubis from Eritrea and Ethiopia carry maternally inherited mitochondria that are closely related to P. hamadryas mitochondria and P. anubis in Kenya and Tanzania carry mitochondria closely related to P. cynocephalus mitochondria, indicating that male introgression by P. anubis might be the major form of hybridization.
